How to Remove Your Name from Google Search Results: What Can Go and What Stays

By RMA — Web Reputation Agency

You cannot remove your name from Google as such, but you can remove or delist many of the results that appear when someone searches for it. Personal contact data, intimate or impersonating content, and outdated information about a private person usually qualify; recent news of public interest and official records usually do not. The most reliable outcome comes from combining targeted removals with new, accurate results that you control.

What it really means to remove your name from Google

Google does not hold a file on you that can be deleted. A search for your name returns pages published by other websites, and each of those pages is a separate case with its own owner, legal basis and chance of success. Removing your name therefore means working result by result.

Two mechanisms are involved. Removal at the source happens when the website deletes or edits the page, after which Google drops it from every search. Delisting happens when Google agrees to stop showing a URL for searches on your name, while the page itself remains online and may still be found through other queries. Our article on the difference between removal, deindexing and suppression explains the practical consequences of each.

Results that can usually be removed

Several categories of content have clear routes in Italy and across the EU, either through Google's own policies or through data protection law. The table summarises the most common ones.

Type of resultMain route
Home address, phone number, personal email, ID numbersGoogle “Results about you” and personal information removal policy
Intimate images shared without consent, explicit deepfakesDedicated Google removal request, plus a report to the platform
Outdated or irrelevant information about a private personRight-to-be-forgotten request under GDPR art. 17
Fake profiles and impersonationImpersonation report to the platform hosting the profile
Content you published yourselfDeletion at source, then the outdated content tool in Search Console
Content found unlawful by a court or authorityLegal removal request to Google with the decision attached

Requests based on the right to be forgotten (diritto all'oblio) follow the Google Spain ruling of the EU Court of Justice (C-131/12). Google balances your privacy against the public interest, considering time elapsed, your role in public life and the nature of the information. If it refuses, you can file a complaint with the Garante per la protezione dei dati personali or go to court. For people acquitted or whose case was dismissed, the Riforma Cartabia (art. 64-ter disp. att. c.p.p.) adds a court annotation that supports the request.

Results that usually stay

Some content will remain visible however strong the wish to delete your name from Google, because the law protects other interests. Knowing this early saves months of fruitless requests and keeps the effort on results that can change.

  • Recent, accurate news of public interest, especially about people with a public role such as politicians, executives or well-known professionals.
  • Official public registers, for example the Italian business register (Registro delle imprese) or professional rolls, when the data is correct and required by law.
  • Honest reviews and criticism of your professional activity, which fall under freedom of expression even when unpleasant.
  • Content about your public statements or activities that you chose to make public, as long as it is accurate.

Even in these cases something can often be done: an article may be updated with later developments, a review that contains false facts or insults may breach platform policies, and a register entry with wrong data can be corrected.

How to proceed, step by step

Begin by mapping the results, then work from the easiest and most certain actions towards the slower ones. A methodical order avoids duplicated effort and gives early results that motivate the rest.

  1. Search your name on google.it in a private window, with and without your city and profession, and list every result on the first two pages.
  2. Delete or edit everything you control: old social accounts, forum posts, profiles on sites you no longer use.
  3. Write to the owners of other websites asking for removal or correction, citing GDPR art. 17 when personal data is involved and keeping a copy of every message.
  4. Use Google's tools: “Results about you” for contact data, the outdated content tool for pages already changed, and the personal information removal forms for other categories.
  5. File right-to-be-forgotten requests for the remaining URLs that qualify, one argument per URL.
  6. Escalate refusals to the Garante or, for content that is defamatory under art. 595 c.p., to legal action.

Patience is part of the method. Website owners and Google often take several weeks to answer, and some requests need a reasoned second attempt with additional documents.

Why removal alone is rarely enough

When someone asks how to remove my name from Google search, they usually want a different first impression, not an empty page. Even after successful removals, the freed positions are filled by whatever else Google finds, which may be another unwanted result or a page about someone else with the same name.

The answer is to build accurate content that you control and that ranks for your name: a complete LinkedIn profile, a personal or professional website, an author page, interviews, publications and profiles on reputable platforms in your field. These results occupy page one, push remaining negative items down and make future problems less visible. For an architect in Florence or a consultant in Milan, this work often has more impact on clients than any single removal.

Removal clears specific results; building fills page one. Lasting control over your name needs both.

Homonyms and other special situations

A frequent problem in Italy is not content about you but about a namesake, for instance someone with the same name involved in a criminal case. You have no legal right to remove accurate content about another person, so the only route is to make your own results clearly distinguishable: consistent use of a middle name or initial, photos, city and profession across all profiles.

Other situations need specific handling: content involving minors, which Google treats with particular care; private information published as part of harassment, which may also justify a report to the Polizia Postale; and old news covered by special rules for criminal records.
